albuterol-salbutamol.summary: The standard asthma rescue inhaler that some bodybuilders use during cuts to get leaner while holding onto muscle.

quick.overview:
Albuterol (salbutamol) is the common asthma rescue inhaler. Some recreational bodybuilders use it, along with other beta-2 agonists, to get leaner and keep muscle while cutting.

It activates beta-2 adrenergic receptors, raising cAMP, a signal also involved in fat breakdown and muscle effects. Oral use has been studied for muscle wasting and obesity, and human studies reported more lean mass and less fat mass. Its main studied purpose is relieving bronchospasm in asthma and COPD, and trials in healthy people seeking cosmetic changes were not found.
quick.how: In bodybuilding circles it is used during cutting phases, alongside a calorie deficit and training, with the aim of fat loss while keeping muscle. Most people know it as the inhaler form; the lean-mass studies used oral dosing. Users describe it as a cutting-phase add-on rather than a standalone fix.
quick.risks: Common effects are tremor, anxiety, headache, cramps, dry mouth and palpitations. Higher doses can cause fast heart rate, arrhythmia and low potassium. Asthma research has examined links between heavy beta-agonist use and asthma death. It is prescription-only in the US, UK and Canada, and beta-2 agonists are regulated in sport.

angle.text: Albuterol activates beta-2 receptors, which raises metabolic rate and is tied to lean-mass effects, so some bodybuilders use it for a leaner, more muscular look during cuts. Small studies of oral dosing reported more lean mass and less fat mass; its studied purpose is bronchospasm.

terbutaline.summary: A prescription asthma beta-2 agonist that physique forums group with albuterol and clenbuterol as a possible aid to leanness.

quick.overview:
Terbutaline is a prescription asthma reliever that physique forums place in the same family as albuterol and clenbuterol, as a possible aid to getting leaner.

It selectively stimulates beta-2 receptors, raising cAMP, and the family is associated with higher metabolic rate. It has been studied for preventing and reversing bronchospasm; trials for fat loss or muscle have not been published.
quick.how: It comes as tablets and injection, and as an inhaler outside the US. In appearance discussion it is mentioned as one of several beta-2 agonists people consider for leanness. Its documented use is as an asthma reliever.
quick.risks: The label lists nervousness, tremor, headache, palpitations and fast heart rate. It carries an FDA boxed warning against use for preterm labour after maternal deaths and serious cardiac events. It is prescription-only, and WADA prohibits it except inhaled with a therapeutic use exemption.

angle.text: Terbutaline is a beta-2 agonist that physique forums group with albuterol and clenbuterol as a route to a leaner look through a higher metabolic rate. Its studied purpose is bronchospasm in asthma.

rimonabant-acomplia.summary: A prescription weight-loss pill that blocks the CB1 receptor to cut appetite; it produced weight loss in trials but was withdrawn in 2008 over mood effects.

quick.overview:
Rimonabant (Acomplia) was an oral prescription weight-loss pill that cut appetite by blocking the cannabinoid-1 receptor, the pathway involved in THC-driven hunger. The payoff was less eating, weight loss and a leaner look.

In large trials, people taking it alongside diet and exercise lost more weight than those on placebo, with improvements in waist circumference and lipid measures. It was approved in the EU in 2006, rejected by the FDA in 2007 and withdrawn worldwide after psychiatric adverse events were reported.
quick.how: It was taken as a daily pill under prescription, combined with diet and exercise. It is no longer marketed, so it is discussed today mainly as a past example of pharmaceutical fat loss.
quick.risks: Trials and post-marketing data linked it to depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation, and the EMA recommended suspension in October 2008. It is no longer legally marketed in the EU, Brazil or India and was never approved in the US.

angle.text: Rimonabant blocked the CB1 receptor to reduce appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Large trials showed more weight loss than placebo, and it was withdrawn in 2008 over mood effects.

lorcaserin-belviq.summary: An FDA-approved prescription weight-loss pill (Belviq) that curbed appetite and modestly outperformed placebo in trials; withdrawn in 2020 over a cancer signal.

quick.overview:
Lorcaserin (Belviq) was a prescription pill for chronic weight management, approved in the US in 2012. It was taken to eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It activates serotonin 5-HT2C receptors in the hypothalamus, thought to increase feelings of fullness. In placebo-controlled trials of nearly 8,000 participants it produced roughly 3 to 3.7 percent more weight loss than placebo over up to a year, with diet and exercise counseling.
quick.how: It was prescribed as a daily pill alongside diet and exercise counseling. It is no longer marketed in the US, so it is discussed as a past weight-loss option.
quick.risks: In 2020 the FDA requested withdrawal after a large safety trial (CAMELLIA-TIMI 61) found more cancer diagnoses among users than on placebo. Doses above the approved range have produced hallucinogenic effects, and the DEA classified it as Schedule IV.

angle.text: Lorcaserin activated serotonin 5-HT2C receptors to increase fullness and reduce eating, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Trials showed modest weight loss compared with placebo, and it was withdrawn in 2020 over a cancer signal.

fenfluramine-phentermine-fen-phen.summary: A 1990s prescription pairing of two appetite suppressants used for weight loss; withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve damage was linked to it.

quick.overview:
Fen-phen was the nickname for taking fenfluramine and phentermine together to lose weight in the 1990s. It was used to cut appetite, shed weight and get leaner.

Fenfluramine mainly releases serotonin and phentermine mainly releases norepinephrine, and together they suppress appetite. A 1984 trial reported greater weight loss than placebo, and use grew widely through the 1990s.
quick.how: It was prescribed as a two-drug combination for weight loss. It is no longer available, and it is cited today as a historical diet-drug example and as the reason later serotonergic obesity drugs were screened for valve safety.
quick.risks: In 1997 reports of heart valve abnormalities led the FDA to request withdrawal of fenfluramine and dexfenfluramine, and the episode produced tens of thousands of lawsuits. Documented harms are valvular heart disease and pulmonary hypertension, attributed to fenfluramine's activation of 5-HT2B receptors on heart valves.

angle.text: Fen-phen paired two appetite suppressants that act on serotonin and norepinephrine, so people ate less and lost weight. It produced weight loss in its era and was withdrawn in 1997 after heart valve problems.

dexfenfluramine-redux.summary: A 1990s serotonin-acting diet pill that cut appetite for weight loss; pulled from the market in 1997 after heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.

quick.overview:
Dexfenfluramine (Redux) was a prescription diet pill approved in the US in the mid-1990s for obesity. It reduced appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner look.

It raises serotonin signalling in the brain by releasing serotonin and blocking its reuptake. Controlled trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined long-term treatment in obesity, and it was widely prescribed, including with phentermine as fen-phen.
quick.how: It was prescribed for obesity alongside diet, either alone or paired with phentermine. It is not available today and appears in discussion as a historical diet drug.
quick.risks: It was withdrawn in September 1997 after heart-valve disease and pulmonary hypertension were reported in users. Pharmacology work linked these harms to activation of the 5-HT2B receptor by its active metabolite. It is not marketed anywhere.

angle.text: Dexfenfluramine increased serotonin signalling to reduce appetite, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Trials examined it for obesity, and it was pulled in 1997 over heart-valve and lung-pressure harms.

phenylpropanolamine.summary: A former over-the-counter decongestant and diet-pill stimulant that suppressed appetite; removed from the market in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.

quick.overview:
Phenylpropanolamine (PPA) was a stimulant-like ingredient in cold remedies and over-the-counter diet pills such as Dexatrim and Acutrim. People took it to eat less and lose weight.

It releases norepinephrine from nerve endings, tightening blood vessels in the nose and, at higher doses, acting on the brain to reduce appetite. Some studies showed weight loss with it.
quick.how: It was sold as a diet aid and decongestant, usually as a pill. It is no longer a mainstream product and is mentioned today as a former diet-pill ingredient.
quick.risks: It raises blood pressure and heart rate, and a 2000 case-control study linked it to hemorrhagic stroke. The FDA advised against its use in November 2000, and the US, Canada and Australia withdrew it in the following years. It is regulated in the US as an amphetamine precursor.

angle.text: Phenylpropanolamine was a stimulant diet-pill ingredient that suppressed appetite so people ate fewer calories and lost weight. It was removed from the market in the early 2000s after a hemorrhagic stroke link.

obetrol-amphetamine-salts.summary: The 1960s prescription diet pill of amphetamine and methamphetamine salts that suppressed appetite for weight loss, and the ancestor of Adderall.

quick.overview:
Obetrol was a US prescription diet pill from the 1950s and 1960s combining amphetamine and methamphetamine salts, marketed for obesity. It suppressed appetite to produce weight loss.

It acted through the central nervous system effects typical of amphetamines. The FDA approved it in 1960 and withdrew approval in 1973. A later methamphetamine-free reformulation became Adderall, approved for ADHD in 1996.
quick.how: It was prescribed as a tablet for exogenous obesity. No drug marketed as Obetrol exists today; it is cited as a historical diet pill.
quick.risks: Amphetamines carry misuse and cardiovascular concerns. The 1973 withdrawal cited weak supporting research as well as the speed-epidemic context. It is no longer sold.

angle.text: Obetrol was an amphetamine-based diet pill that suppressed appetite, so people ate less and lost weight. It is of historical interest as the ancestor of Adderall.

cetilistat.summary: An orlistat-style fat-blocking pill that lets some dietary fat pass through unabsorbed; phase 2 data show weight loss and it is mainly available in Japan.

quick.overview:
Cetilistat is a pill that blocks fat-digesting enzymes so some of the fat you eat passes out of the body instead of being absorbed. The aim is fewer calories absorbed and a leaner look.

It inhibits pancreatic and gastrointestinal lipases, so triglycerides are not broken down. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss in obese patients and, in people with type 2 diabetes, weight and HbA1c reductions, with tolerability described as comparable to or better than orlistat.
quick.how: It is taken as a pill with meals and used alongside a calorie-conscious diet. It was developed by Alizyme, Takeda and Norgine and is reportedly approved in Japan, with limited availability elsewhere.
quick.risks: Side effects are digestive, such as oily stools, urgency and flatulence, and absorption of fat-soluble vitamins may be reduced. It is not widely available.

angle.text: Cetilistat blocks intestinal fat digestion so fewer calories are absorbed, leading to weight loss and a leaner look. Phase 2 trials reported weight loss, and it is available mainly in Japan.

plenity-gelesis100.summary: A swallowed gel capsule taken before meals that swells in the stomach to promote fullness and modest weight loss.

quick.overview:
Plenity is a capsule of cross-linked cellulose gel taken with water before meals to help people feel full and eat less, supporting weight loss and a leaner look in adults with overweight or obesity.

The gel absorbs water and swells in the stomach and small intestine, forming a semisolid mass that may promote fullness. The FDA cleared it as a medical device in April 2019. Reviews describe the weight loss as modest, and a 2022 AGA guideline recommended limiting its use to clinical trials.
quick.how: It is taken as capsules with water before meals, alongside normal diet efforts. It is a device, not a drug.
quick.risks: Side effects are mostly mild digestive symptoms. Long-term safety data beyond 24 weeks are limited, and it is contraindicated in pregnancy, malabsorption and cholestasis.

angle.text: Plenity is a gel capsule that swells in the stomach to increase fullness at meals, so you eat less and lose weight. It is cleared as a device and trials show modest weight loss.

hu6.summary: An experimental slow-release prodrug of the fat-burner DNP that makes the body burn more energy as heat; still in phase 2 trials.

quick.overview:
HU6 is an experimental pill from Rivus Pharmaceuticals designed to deliver DNP, a historic fat-burning mitochondrial uncoupler, in a more controlled way. People follow it as a possible safer route to DNP-style fat loss.

After conversion to DNP in the liver, it lets mitochondria lose energy as heat instead of making ATP, so more energy is burned. A 2023 phase 2a trial of 80 people reported reduced liver fat versus placebo over 61 days, and it is in phase 2 trials for fatty liver, obesity and heart failure.
quick.how: It is available only inside clinical trials, as a once-daily pill. It is not sold as a product.
quick.risks: Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were most common in the trial. It is unapproved anywhere. DNP itself was judged too toxic for human consumption, has caused fatal overdoses and is banned for human consumption.

angle.text: HU6 is a slow-release prodrug of DNP that uncouples mitochondria so more energy is burned as heat, aiming at fat loss and a leaner look. A 2023 phase 2a trial reported lower liver fat, and it is not available as a product.

ubt251.summary: Investigational once-weekly GLP-1/GIP/glucagon triple agonist from China, licensed to Novo Nordisk, aimed at appetite and weight loss; phase 2 data exist.

quick.overview:
UBT251 is an experimental injectable peptide that activates the GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors at once. People follow it as a next-generation weight-loss peptide after semaglutide and tirzepatide, aiming at less appetite and a leaner body.

It is designed to combine the appetite and insulin effects of GLP-1 and GIP with the energy-expenditure effects associated with glucagon-receptor activation. Two 24-week phase 2 trials in China were published in 2026, and phase 3 studies are registered. It is being tested for obesity, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease, sleep apnea and fatty liver disease.
quick.how: It is given as a once-weekly injection and is available only inside clinical trials. Novo Nordisk holds a licence for development outside China.
quick.risks: Safety data are limited to early trials. The wider drug class is associated with gastrointestinal side effects. It is not approved in any jurisdiction.

angle.text: UBT251 activates GLP-1, GIP and glucagon receptors to reduce appetite and raise energy use, aiming at weight loss and a leaner look. Phase 2 trials have reported, and it is not an approved or prescribable drug.

benzphetamine.summary: A prescription amphetamine-type appetite suppressant that cuts hunger for short-term weight loss; Schedule III and labelled for a few weeks of use.

quick.overview:
Benzphetamine (Didrex) is an older prescription appetite suppressant related to amphetamine. It reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

It is thought to increase norepinephrine and dopamine release in the brain's feeding centers, and the body converts it to amphetamine and methamphetamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a reduced-calorie diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher.
quick.how: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period alongside a calorie-restricted diet. The label states it is not for long-term use.
quick.risks: Reported effects include raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia and restlessness. The label cites an association between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension and contraindicates use in pregnancy. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US.

angle.text: Benzphetamine is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is a prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

phendimetrazine.summary: An older prescription stimulant appetite suppressant that cuts hunger for short-term weight loss; controlled and labelled for a few weeks of use.

quick.overview:
Phendimetrazine (Bontril) is an older prescription stimulant that suppresses appetite, so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

About 30 percent of an oral dose is converted in the body to phenmetrazine, which releases norepinephrine and dopamine. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher. Published clinical evidence for obesity is older and sparse.
quick.how: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a short period with a reduced-calorie diet. It is mentioned alongside other older prescription appetite suppressants.
quick.risks: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, insomnia, agitation and other stimulant effects, and cites a link between long-term anorectic use and pulmonary hypertension. Safe use in pregnancy is not established. It is Schedule III in the US.

angle.text: Phendimetrazine is a stimulant that suppresses appetite, so calorie intake falls and weight comes down. It is an older prescription obesity medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

diethylpropion.summary: An older prescription appetite suppressant that cuts hunger for short-term weight loss; Schedule IV in the US and recommended for withdrawal in the EU.

quick.overview:
Diethylpropion (amfepramone) is an older prescription appetite suppressant that reduces hunger so people eat less and lose weight, working toward a leaner look.

The body converts it to ethcathinone, which mainly affects norepinephrine signalling. In the US it is labelled as a short-term add-on, lasting a few weeks, to a calorie-restricted diet for people with a BMI of 30 or higher. Meta-analyses of weight-loss drugs have included it alongside phentermine and sibutramine.
quick.how: It is taken as a pill under prescription for a few weeks alongside dieting. It is discussed with other older diet drugs.
quick.risks: The label lists raised heart rate and blood pressure, arrhythmia and rare pulmonary hypertension, with a cited association for anorectic use beyond three months. It is Schedule IV in the US, and in June 2022 the EMA's safety committee recommended withdrawing it from the EU market.

angle.text: Diethylpropion is a stimulant appetite suppressant that lowers calorie intake and leads to weight loss and a leaner look. It is an older prescription medication labelled for a few weeks of use.

pioglitazone.summary: A prescription type 2 diabetes drug known to raise subcutaneous fat, which is why it comes up in talk about body-fat distribution.

quick.overview:
Pioglitazone is a generic prescription pill for type 2 diabetes. It comes up in appearance discussion because it is known to raise subcutaneous fat, which people connect to changing where body fat sits.

It activates PPAR-gamma receptors, mainly in fat tissue, muscle and liver, which lowers insulin resistance, and weight gain from added subcutaneous fat is a recognised effect. No human study has tested it for cosmetic purposes.
quick.how: Its documented use is as a daily diabetes pill under prescription. In one forum context it has also been discussed as a topical under-eye product.
quick.risks: The label has a boxed warning for congestive heart failure and lists edema and fractures. Bladder cancer warnings were added in 2011. It is prescription only, and no cosmetic use is approved.

angle.text: Pioglitazone is known to raise subcutaneous fat storage, so appearance discussions bring it up in connection with changing body-fat distribution. It is studied for type 2 diabetes, and no human study has tested cosmetic use.

anamorelin.summary: An oral ghrelin-receptor drug that raised lean body mass in cancer cachexia trials; muscle-focused users follow it.

quick.overview:
Anamorelin is an experimental oral drug that mimics ghrelin, the hunger hormone. Muscle-focused users follow it because it raised lean body mass in trials, pointing toward a fuller, more muscular physique.

It activates the ghrelin receptor in the brain and pituitary, increasing appetite and prompting growth hormone and IGF-1 release. Phase 3 trials in lung cancer patients (ROMANA 1 and 2) reported gains in lean body mass without clear gains in grip strength. It is approved in Japan for cachexia, and European regulators declined authorisation in 2017.
quick.how: It is a pill taken daily in cancer-cachexia trials and in Japan under prescription. It is discussed in appearance contexts as one of several ghrelin-mimetic growth hormone secretagogues.
quick.risks: Safety data come from cancer-patient trials, and EU regulators cited inadequate safety recording. It is prescription-only and not marketed in most countries, and it is on the WADA prohibited list.

angle.text: Anamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor to raise appetite and growth hormone, which in trials increased lean body mass and points toward a fuller physique. Those trials were in cancer patients, and no trial has tested it for physique goals.

macimorelin.summary: An oral ghrelin-receptor agonist that triggers growth hormone release, approved as a one-time diagnostic test for adult GH deficiency.

quick.overview:
Macimorelin (Macrilen) is an oral drug that stimulates the pituitary to release growth hormone. GH-minded users note it as a secretagogue, with the idea that more GH could mean more muscle and a leaner look.

It binds the ghrelin receptor in the pituitary and hypothalamus, prompting a pulse of growth hormone that can be measured. The FDA approved it in December 2017 as a diagnostic test for adult growth hormone deficiency, not as a treatment, and no study has tested it for appearance.
quick.how: Doctors give a single oral dose in clinic and measure GH levels afterwards. It is discussed in looksmaxxing-adjacent circles as one of the ghrelin-mimetic secretagogues.
quick.risks: The label lists altered taste, dizziness, headache and nausea as common reactions and warns of QT prolongation. Strong CYP3A4 inducers can distort test results.

angle.text: Macimorelin stimulates growth hormone release through the ghrelin receptor, and GH-minded users link that to more muscle and a leaner look. It is approved only as a one-time diagnostic for adult GH deficiency, and no study has tested it for appearance.

capromorelin.summary: An oral ghrelin agonist sold as a pet appetite stimulant that also raises growth hormone; a human older-adult trial showed a small lean-mass gain.

quick.overview:
Capromorelin is a Pfizer-developed oral drug that mimics ghrelin, raising appetite and growth hormone. It draws interest as a growth hormone secretagogue that could support lean mass and a fuller look.

It activates the ghrelin receptor, raising growth hormone and IGF-1 levels. A trial in older adults with mild functional limitation reported a small lean-mass gain, and human development was then discontinued. It is sold for pets as Entyce (dogs, US 2016) and Elura (cats with kidney disease, US 2020).
quick.how: Its real-world use is veterinary, as an appetite stimulant for dogs and cats. In people it has been used only in clinical trials.
quick.risks: It is a veterinary prescription drug, with vomiting and diarrhoea noted in animals. Human safety data are limited to early-phase and older-adult trials, and it is not approved for humans.

angle.text: Capromorelin activates the ghrelin receptor to raise appetite and growth hormone, which points toward more lean mass and a fuller look. A human older-adult trial reported a small lean-mass gain, and no study has tested it for appearance.

relamorelin.summary: An injected ghrelin analogue developed for diabetic gastroparesis that some group with ghrelin-pathway appetite and muscle compounds.

quick.overview:
Relamorelin (RM-131) is an investigational injected ghrelin analogue. Some people group it with ghrelin-pathway compounds associated with appetite, growth hormone and lean mass.

It is a synthetic pentapeptide that activates the ghrelin receptor, which raises growth hormone and appetite. It was developed to speed stomach emptying in diabetic gastroparesis, and phase 2 trials reported faster emptying and less vomiting. It was also studied in constipation and anorexia nervosa. Phase 3 trials registered in 2017 and 2018 were all later terminated.
quick.how: It has been given as a subcutaneous injection inside clinical trials only. It is not sold as a product.
quick.risks: It is not approved anywhere. Safety data come from clinical trials in gastrointestinal and eating-disorder patients, and no studies have tested it for appearance.

angle.text: Relamorelin activates the ghrelin receptor to raise appetite and growth hormone signalling, and some link that to more lean mass and a fuller look. It was studied for diabetic gastroparesis, and no appearance data exist.
